::: {.why}
The two equations you solved last night are the entire Black-Scholes argument, and doing it in one step first means the continuous version is notation rather than a new idea.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Derive the one-step binomial option price from the replicating portfolio, with no probability anywhere in the argument.
- Say why the real probability of an up move does not appear in the answer, and what does appear instead.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Do the one-step derivation cleanly on paper: the hedge ratio is the ratio of the option payoff spread to the stock price spread, and the price is the cost of the replicating portfolio. Note that you never used the probability of an up move, which is the fact that surprises everyone and is the whole content of risk-neutral pricing.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Extend to n steps and take the limit: implement a binomial tree in qlib/derivatives/tree.py with the standard up and down factors, price a European call, and show it converges to a limit as the number of steps grows. Plot the convergence and note that it oscillates.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Read off the risk-neutral probability from the one-step formula and note that it is the probability that makes the stock's expected return equal the risk-free rate. That observation is tomorrow's subject and it is worth arriving at from the algebra rather than being told.
:::
:::
